newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain spars with Catalan allies over 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Spain spars with Catalan allies over 1997 budget.

text.p: The Spanish government and its Catalan allies were confronting each other on Wednesday on the details of the 1997 budget, with neither side willing to climb down just two weeks before the draft must be presented to parliament.

The Catalan Convergence and Unity (CiU) coalition is demanding more health funds from the central government in return for their 16 votes which will get the budget parliamentary approval. But they went home empty-handed from a four-hour meeting in Madrid late on Tuesday.
"We can't address all needs, not all of those of the autonomous communities," Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar told a local radio station.
Both groups have agreed in principle to a rigorous budget that will cut the deficit and propel Spain into the group of nations launching the European common currency in 1999.
But the talks have stumbled on health financing, and both sides appeared to be digging in their heels.

At stake for the Catalans is the repayment of 60 billion pesetas ($471.3 million) the central government owes the region for health care, and of which the Catalans demand that 32 billion be paid back in 1997.
But Aznar said his four-month-old Popular Party government had already done all it could do.
"I hope that everyone is reasonable (and understands this)," he said.

The health component of the overall budget is projected to grow by six percent, while overall budget expenditure will not grow by more than two percent, he said. But that won't be enough to meet all health needs, he added.
"We are prepared to devote to health all the means we can," Aznar said.
But the Catalans appeared to be hardening their stance on this particular issue.
"If this doesn't happen (if the money isn't forthcoming) then there won't be agreement on the budget this year," the CiU's economic spokesman told Spanish radio.
The CiU voted against the previous administration on the 1996 budget, prompting early elections that ousted the Socialists after 13 years in power.
Other Catalan demands this round include independent administration of minor policies, fiscal incentives for small companies and certain taxation powers.
Despite the tough talk, a spokesman for the Economy Ministry said on Tuesday that he expected the Catalans eventually to support the government.
